title: Falling Tiles Settle
statement:
A row of upright tiles is described by a string row. Each character is one tile: 'L' means it was just tipped to the left, 'R' means it was just tipped to the right, and '.' means it is still standing.

Every second, each falling tile pushes its neighbour on the side it is falling toward, and that neighbour starts falling the same way one second later. A standing tile pushed from both sides at the same second stays upright. A tile that has already fallen never changes.

Return the row after everything has stopped moving, using the same three characters.

examples.why: The R and the L close in on three tiles. The outer two fall toward their nearer pusher; the middle one is hit from both sides at once and stays up. Nothing pushes the first two tiles.
The tile at index 1 is pushed from both sides at once. The tile at index 3 sits between an L falling away and an R falling away, so nothing touches it.
The L knocks over the tile on its left; the R knocks over everything to its right.

hints: Only the nearest falling tile on each side of a standing tile can reach it. What are the possible combinations of those two?
Split the row at every L or R. Each stretch of dots sits between two letters (pretend there is an L before the start and an R after the end). L…L fills with L, R…R fills with R, L…R stays standing.
For R…L, walk two pointers inward from both ends, writing R on the left and L on the right. If they meet on one tile, it stays '.'.

explain.intuition:
A standing tile can only be reached by the closest letter on each side, because any letter further away would have to push through that closer one first. So cut the row into stretches of dots, each bounded by two letters, and decide each stretch on its own.

There are four cases. L…L: the right L sweeps everything left, so all dots become L. R…R: all become R. L…R: both fall away, nothing moves. R…L: the two fronts travel toward each other at the same speed, so the left half becomes R, the right half becomes L, and with an odd count the exact middle tile is hit from both sides and stays up. Two pointers walking inward fill this case naturally. Adding an imaginary L in front and an R at the end makes the edges ordinary cases.
steps: Wrap the row as 'L' + row + 'R' and convert it to an array.
Walk left to right, remembering the index prev of the last letter.

At each new letter i: if both letters match, fill the dots between with that letter. If it is R then L, move lo = prev + 1 and hi = i − 1 inward, writing R at lo and L at hi, while lo < hi. If it is L then R, do nothing.
Drop the two sentinels and join.
pitfalls: Filling with lo ≤ hi in the R…L case, which knocks over the middle tile that should stay standing.
Updating the row in place during a second-by-second simulation. A tile tipped this second must not push its neighbour until the next one.
Letting a leading run of dots fall right or a trailing run fall left. Nothing pushes from outside the row.

solutions.title: Simulate second by second
solutions.idea: Build each new row from the previous one. A dot falls right if its left neighbour is R and its right one is not L, and the mirror for L. Stop when nothing changes.

solutions.title: Segments between letters
solutions.idea: Each stretch of dots depends only on the letters at its two ends. Fill it by case, with two pointers for R…L.

followups: Return the second at which each tile falls, or -1 if it never does.
Solve it with two passes that record the distance to the nearest R on the left and nearest L on the right. When is that easier to explain?
